title: A paternoster lift never stops: you step into an open cabin as it passes

cover.alt: Two open, doorless wooden lift cabins side by side in a panelled wall, one rising and one sinking past the floor.

body: A **paternoster** is a chain of open compartments, each usually built for two people, that moves slowly and endlessly in a loop, up one shaft and down the other, without ever stopping. The cabins have no doors. You wait for a cabin to come level with the floor, step in, and step out again at the floor you want. The first ones were installed in Liverpool in 1868, and they were popular for decades because they could carry more passengers than ordinary lifts.

slides.alt: In a panelled wall, open wooden lift cabins glide past without stopping, rising in one shaft and sinking in the other.
slides.caption: Vienna City Hall: empty, doorless cabins glide past without stopping, rising in one shaft and sinking in the other.

slides.prompt: Why is this kind of lift called a paternoster?
slides.detail: Pater noster are the prayer's first two words in Latin. The endless loop of cabins reminded people of rosary beads, used to count prayers.

slides.label: a paternoster's typical speed
slides.text: Slower than a stroll, so that passengers can step on and off a moving cabin.

slides.heading: Where paternosters survive
slides.note: Those outside Europe are one each in Malaysia, Sri Lanka and Peru

slides.question: Why did many countries stop allowing new paternosters?
slides.explanation: Their accident rate is estimated at about 30 times that of ordinary lifts. Elderly and disabled people and children are most at risk.
